definition: The complex vector space with an inner product in which quantum states live; for n qubits it has dimension 2ⁿ.
A matrix equal to its own conjugate transpose. Its eigenvalues are real, so it can represent an observable or a Hamiltonian.
A matrix whose conjugate transpose is its inverse. Unitaries preserve inner products; time evolution and quantum gates are unitary.
Every Hermitian matrix can be written as V diag(λ) V† with real eigenvalues λ and an orthonormal eigenbasis V.
[A, B] = AB − BA. It vanishes exactly when A and B commute; non-zero commutators give uncertainty relations and Trotter error.
The matrix form of the tensor product: an mn × mn block matrix whose blocks are A_ij B. It combines states and operators of separate systems.
A column vector |ψ⟩ representing a quantum state in Dirac notation.
The conjugate transpose ⟨ψ| of a ket; a bra and a ket together give an inner product ⟨φ|ψ⟩.
The bra-ket notation for quantum states and operators: |ψ⟩ for states, ⟨φ|ψ⟩ for inner products, |ψ⟩⟨φ| for outer products.
A linear combination of basis states with complex amplitudes. Unlike a random mixture, it has definite relative phases that other measurements can detect.
A complex coefficient of a state in some basis; its squared modulus is the probability of that outcome.
An overall factor e^{iγ} on a state. It changes no measurement outcome, so states differing only by it are physically identical.
A phase between components of a superposition. Unlike a global phase it is measurable, though not by measuring in the basis it sits in.
Measuring |ψ⟩ in an orthonormal basis gives outcome k with probability |⟨e_k|ψ⟩|².
After a measurement the state is replaced by the (normalised) projection onto the observed outcome.
One run of a quantum experiment ending in a measurement; expectation values are estimated by averaging many shots.
A Hermitian operator representing a measurable quantity; its eigenvalues are the possible measurement results.
The average result of measuring an observable A on many copies of a state: ⟨A⟩ = ⟨ψ|A|ψ⟩, or Tr(Aρ) for a density matrix.
For any state, σ_A σ_B ≥ |⟨[A, B]⟩|/2 (Robertson). Non-commuting observables cannot both be sharp.
A two-level quantum system with basis states |0⟩ and |1⟩.
The unit sphere on which every pure qubit state sits, with coordinates (⟨X⟩, ⟨Y⟩, ⟨Z⟩). Mixed states fill its interior, the Bloch ball.
The vector (⟨X⟩, ⟨Y⟩, ⟨Z⟩) of a qubit state; length 1 for pure states, less for mixed ones.
The three 2 × 2 matrices X, Y and Z: Hermitian, unitary, squaring to the identity and pairwise anticommuting.
A tensor product of one Pauli matrix or identity per qubit; the 4ⁿ strings form a basis for operators on n qubits.
R_P(θ) = exp(−iθP/2): a rotation of the Bloch sphere by θ about the axis of the Pauli P.
The single-qubit gate (X + Z)/√2, which exchanges the Z and X bases.
The controlled-NOT gate: flips the target qubit when the control is |1⟩. With single-qubit rotations it is universal.
One of four maximally entangled two-qubit states, such as (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.
Approximating exp(−i(A+B)t) by repeating short steps exp(−iAt/r)exp(−iBt/r); the error shrinks as the steps get shorter.
The Hermitian operator for a system's energy; it generates time evolution through U(t) = exp(−iHt).
i d|ψ⟩/dt = H|ψ⟩ (with ħ = 1), whose solution is |ψ(t)⟩ = exp(−iHt)|ψ(0)⟩.
An eigenvector of the Hamiltonian; under time evolution it only acquires a phase, so it is stationary.
Rotation of a spin's Bloch vector about the field axis; for H = hZ the angular frequency is 2h.
Periodic population transfer in a driven two-level system; on resonance the population swings fully between |0⟩ and |1⟩.
The description in which observables evolve, A(t) = U†AU, while the state stays fixed; it gives the same predictions as the Schrödinger picture.
An observable that commutes with the Hamiltonian; its probability distribution never changes under the evolution.
A block of the state space labelled by the value of a conserved quantity; the dynamics never connects different blocks.
The oscillator operator a with a|n⟩ = √n|n−1⟩; its adjoint a† is the creation operator, and [a, a†] = 1.
A state of definite quanta number |n⟩ of an oscillator mode, eigenstate of a†a.
An eigenstate of the annihilation operator, a|α⟩ = α|α⟩: Poisson photon numbers with mean |α|² and minimum quadrature noise.
The oscillator's position-like x = (a + a†)/√2 or momentum-like p = i(a† − a)/√2 operators, measured by homodyne detection.
A correlation of a multi-part pure state that cannot be written as a product of states of the parts.
Writing a two-party pure state as Σ λ_k |a_k⟩|b_k⟩ with orthonormal bases on each side; the number of non-zero λ_k is the Schmidt rank.
The operation that discards part of a composite system, leaving the reduced density matrix of the rest.
The density matrix of a subsystem, obtained by the partial trace; it reproduces every measurement on that subsystem.
The von Neumann entropy of either half of a pure bipartite state: 0 for a product, 1 bit for a Bell pair.
ρ = Σ p_j |ψ_j⟩⟨ψ_j|: the description of a possibly mixed state, Hermitian, positive and of trace 1, with ⟨A⟩ = Tr(Aρ).
A state that is not a single pure vector: a statistical mixture, or part of a larger entangled system. Its Bloch vector is shorter than 1.
Tr ρ², equal to 1 for pure states and down to 1/d for the maximally mixed state.
The density matrix I/d: every outcome equally likely in every basis, the centre of the Bloch ball.
The spin chain H = −J Σ Z_i Z_{i+1} − h Σ X_i, with a quantum phase transition at h = J.
A mapping of a one-dimensional chain of spins onto fermions; nearest-neighbour XY and transverse-field Ising chains become free fermions.

The complete description of a quantum system: a unit vector |ψ⟩ in Hilbert space (up to a global phase), or a density matrix when the state is mixed. Every prediction about measurements follows from it.
⟨φ|ψ⟩, the complex number comparing two states: the sum of φ's conjugated components times ψ's. |⟨φ|ψ⟩|² is the probability that a system in |ψ⟩ is found in |φ⟩; zero means the states are orthogonal.
The length of a vector, ‖ψ‖ = √⟨ψ|ψ⟩. Physical states are normalised to length 1 so their Born-rule probabilities add up to 1.
A set of unit vectors that are pairwise orthogonal and span the space. The possible outcomes of a measurement form one, and any state is a unique combination of its vectors.
The basis |0⟩, |1⟩ for one qubit and the bit strings |00…0⟩ to |11…1⟩ for n qubits: the eigenbasis of the Z operators and the basis hardware measures in by default.

The orthonormal basis whose vectors are a measurement's outcomes. Hardware measures in the computational basis, so measuring in another basis means rotating the state first (a Hadamard turns an X measurement into a Z measurement).
A number λ with A|v⟩ = λ|v⟩ for some nonzero vector |v⟩. For an observable the eigenvalues are the possible measurement results, and for a Hamiltonian they are the energies.
A nonzero vector that a matrix only rescales, A|v⟩ = λ|v⟩. An eigenstate of an observable gives that observable's value with certainty.
An orthonormal basis made of a matrix's eigenvectors. Every Hermitian or unitary matrix has one, and in it the matrix is diagonal.
The set of an operator's eigenvalues. An observable's spectrum lists its possible outcomes; a Hamiltonian's spectrum lists the allowed energies.
When two or more independent eigenvectors share one eigenvalue. Measuring a degenerate outcome does not single out a vector, only the subspace (eigenspace) it spans.
A†, the matrix transposed with every entry complex-conjugated. It turns a ket into its bra, and defines Hermitian (A† = A) and unitary (U†U = I) matrices.
|ψ⟩⟨φ|, a ket times a bra, which is a matrix rather than a number. |ψ⟩⟨ψ| is the projector onto |ψ⟩ and the density matrix of the pure state |ψ⟩.
An operator P with P² = P = P†. It keeps the part of a vector inside one subspace and removes the rest; measurement outcomes correspond to projectors onto eigenspaces.
The textbook measurement: outcome k occurs with probability ⟨ψ|P_k|ψ⟩ for projectors P_k that sum to the identity, and the state jumps to the normalised P_k|ψ⟩.
Tr A, the sum of a matrix's diagonal entries, which equals the sum of its eigenvalues. A density matrix has trace 1, and Tr(ρA) is the expectation value of A.
e^A = I + A + A²/2! + …, computed in practice by diagonalising A and exponentiating its eigenvalues. e^(−iHt) is how a Hamiltonian becomes a unitary.
U(t) = e^(−iHt/ħ), the unitary that carries a state from time 0 to time t under a time-independent Hamiltonian: |ψ(t)⟩ = U(t)|ψ(0)⟩.
How an isolated system changes in time: by a unitary operator, so norms, inner products and purity are preserved and the evolution can always be undone.
The constant ħ ≈ 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s that converts energy into angular frequency, E = ħω. Theory usually sets ħ = 1, so energies and frequencies are measured in the same units.
The eigenstate of a Hamiltonian with the lowest energy.
Any energy eigenstate above the ground state; for a qubit, usually |1⟩.
One of the allowed energies of a system, an eigenvalue of its Hamiltonian. Differences between levels set the frequencies the system responds to.
In quantum dynamics, driving a transition at the frequency matching the gap between two energy levels; at resonance a Rabi oscillation swings the full population between them.
The difference Δ between a drive's frequency and a transition's frequency. A detuned drive gives faster but incomplete Rabi oscillations, of amplitude Ω²/(Ω² + Δ²).
The usual bookkeeping in which states evolve in time and operators stay fixed. It gives the same predictions as the Heisenberg picture.
Observables whose operators commute. They share an eigenbasis, so they can be measured together, from the same shots, without disturbing each other.
Two operators anticommute when AB = −BA, i.e. their anticommutator {A, B} = AB + BA is zero. Different Pauli matrices anticommute.
In quantum mechanics, the spread of an observable's outcomes in a state: ⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩². It is zero exactly when the state is an eigenstate of A.

The short list the theory rests on: states are unit vectors in a Hilbert space, observables are Hermitian operators, outcome probabilities follow the Born rule, measurement updates the state, closed systems evolve unitarily, and composite systems combine by tensor product.
No physical process can copy an unknown quantum state. It is why a quantum state cannot be measured many times from one copy, and so why expectation values need many runs.
A computation written as a sequence of quantum gates on qubit wires, read left to right, usually ending in measurements.
A unitary operation on a few qubits, the quantum counterpart of a logic gate. Unlike most classical gates it is reversible.
A small set of gates, for example arbitrary single-qubit rotations plus CNOT, whose products can approximate any unitary to any accuracy.
A single-qubit gate that leaves |0⟩ alone and multiplies |1⟩ by a phase (i for the S gate, e^(iφ) in general): a rotation about the Z axis up to a global phase.
A two-qubit gate that applies an operation to a target qubit only when a control qubit is |1⟩. CNOT and controlled-Z are the common examples, and either one can create entanglement.
The two-qubit gate that exchanges the states of two qubits, |ab⟩ → |ba⟩. It takes three CNOTs.
A system made of parts, such as several qubits. Its Hilbert space is the tensor product of the parts' spaces, so its dimension is the product of theirs.
An operator that acts on only one part of a composite system, written A ⊗ I. Its expectation value depends only on that part's reduced state.
A state of a composite system that factorises, |ψ⟩ = |a⟩ ⊗ |b⟩: each part has a definite state of its own and there is no entanglement.
A mixed state that is a probabilistic mixture of product states. A state that is not separable is entangled.
A state that can be written as a single vector |ψ⟩; its density matrix |ψ⟩⟨ψ| has purity 1.
Classical uncertainty about which pure state was prepared: |ψ_i⟩ with probability p_i, described by ρ = Σ p_i |ψ_i⟩⟨ψ_i|. Unlike a superposition, it cannot interfere.
The off-diagonal entries of a density matrix in a chosen basis. They carry the relative phases that make interference possible; a statistical mixture in that basis has none.
The loss of coherence as a system becomes correlated with its environment: off-diagonal terms of the density matrix decay and the state drifts toward a statistical mixture.
The mixed state ρ = e^(−βH)/Tr e^(−βH) of a system in equilibrium at inverse temperature β; at zero temperature it becomes the ground state.
A measure of how close two states are: |⟨φ|ψ⟩|² for pure states, 1 when they are equal and 0 when they are orthogonal. It has a general form for mixed states.
The system with Hamiltonian ħω(a†a + 1/2): evenly spaced levels ħω(n + 1/2). It models a mode of light, a mechanical resonator or a superconducting resonator.
n̂ = a†a, the operator that counts quanta in an oscillator mode; the Fock state |n⟩ is its eigenstate with eigenvalue n.
|0⟩, the oscillator's ground state with no quanta; the annihilation operator sends it to zero. It is also the coherent state with zero amplitude.
A Gaussian state whose uncertainty is pushed below the vacuum level in one quadrature at the cost of more in the other, keeping the uncertainty relation satisfied.
A particle or degree of freedom with two levels, described by the Pauli matrices (S = σ/2 with ħ = 1). Mathematically it is a qubit.
Spins coupled through Z_iZ_j terms, so the energy depends only on whether neighbours align. On its own it is classical (diagonal in the computational basis); a transverse field makes it quantum.
A coupling X_iX_j (often with Y_iY_j, the XY model) that swaps excitations between spins. With only nearest-neighbour terms the chain maps to free fermions.
Spins coupled by X_iX_j + Y_iY_j + Z_iZ_j, which is the same in every direction, so the total spin is conserved.
An interaction only between spins next to each other on a chain or lattice. Hardware with fixed qubit connectivity favours it.
A model with as many independent conserved quantities as degrees of freedom, which makes it exactly solvable and keeps it from thermalising; free-fermion chains are the standard example.
Generic many-body dynamics spreading local information into complicated, many-qubit correlations, so that it can no longer be read from any few-qubit observable.
